name: Kira Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: The Work Futures Panel is independent and has no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. What you tell me is confidential. Could you describe a normal shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am Kira Farah, 43, a senior operator at a large mine. I check the loader and route, move ore, and help the next crew read the equipment log; I use AI tools daily to sort shift data, but the machine check is still mine.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what gets difficult?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I enjoy solving a fault with the crew before it turns into a long stoppage. My partner Karim works at a local clinic, and we have two school-age children, a mortgage and a few months of expenses saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a small AI helper can tidy the route notes, but no one should skip checking the loader. I already use tools to compare shift data, and they are useful when a person checks the result.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My job is mostly physical and the card says pay carries on much the same. Karim works at a clinic, so our household is not tied to two mine wages, and we have a few months saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my equipment walk-around and use my tablet to compare the shift plan with actual delays. I would leave the emergency account untouched unless the mine cut hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel comfortable about my own role in this picture. I still watch how the saved minutes are used because the crew needs safe time, not just a faster number.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of your shift would you trust a tool to help with?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would use an AI summary for route delays and maintenance notes, then compare it with the equipment log. The loader needs a person to decide whether a new sound is harmless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children if they asked whether your job is safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my children that I expect to keep operating equipment, but no job is guaranteed forever. They can learn broadly without worrying that this small tool means I am leaving next month.

say: I would try a helper for **route notes**, but keep checking the loader.
I think a person should always check the **result**.
think: My work is mostly **physical**, and the card leaves pay much the same.
I rely on Karim’s clinic wage, so we are not tied to two **mine wages**.
do: Keep my **walk-around** and compare the plan with real delays.
Leave the **emergency account** untouched unless hours fall.
feel: I feel **comfortable** about my role, while watching how saved minutes affect safe work.
S0.quote: The loader needs a person to decide whether a new sound is harmless.
fieldNote: Kira already uses tools to compare shift data, but keeps **safety judgment** with operators.
Her partner has work outside the mine, and savings cover **several months**.
She sees no immediate threat to her own **role** in this mild scenario.

steps.text: Keep the loader walk-around on every shift
Compare route summaries with the equipment log

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team the planning screens will change before the loader itself does. We should use the software to find delays without treating its suggested target as a safety rule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Shift reports and handovers are part of my lead job, so I could lose some desk time. The equipment still needs operators, and I can learn a tool once someone proves it works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join a mine trial of the new maintenance reports and learn how to flag a bad recommendation. I would ask the safety committee to keep an operator review before targets change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the pace, but I see a route to adjust. My main worry is whether the software counts safe inspection time as wasted time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you protect the crew from a target set by software?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the crew to record when the planned target conflicts with a required equipment check. Then we could bring actual examples to the safety committee rather than argue in general.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need to know before using the new tools each shift?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Before using a new screen alone, I would test it against a month of old logs. If it makes the same calls, I would use it for planning but still verify faults in person.

say: I expect planning screens to change before the **loader** does.
I would use software to find delays, not set a **safety rule**.
think: I spend some lead time on reports and **handovers**.
I can learn a tool once someone **proves** it works.
do: Join the mine trial and learn to flag **bad recommendations**.
Ask for an operator review before changing **targets**.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about the pace and how safe inspection time is counted.
S1.quote: We should use the software to find delays without treating its suggested target as a safety rule.
fieldNote: She expects changes in **planning tasks** before physical loading work.
Kira is willing to test tools but retains a human **equipment check**.
Her concern is the incentive to misread **inspection time** as wasted time.

steps.text: Learn the maintenance report tool during the mine trial
Take target concerns to the safety committee

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI could plan shifts by 2028, while robots for loader work come around 2031. The crew needs paid training and a say in where experienced operators go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The thinking part of my lead work could go quickly, though the machine work has a three-year window after AGI. I use AI daily, but I cannot learn my way out of a robot taking the loader job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the mine for its transfer list now and choose a paid equipment-diagnostics course if it leads to an open role. In 2029, I would keep my loader shifts while taking that course and testing its tools on safe practice data.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about how fast the thinking tasks change, but not trapped. We have a few months saved and Karim's clinic job, so I can make a careful move if the mine gives clear terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you and your partner handle the training cost?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Karim and I would check the course schedule against the mortgage and school calendar. I would only use savings for travel if the mine confirmed the course was paid and connected to an actual vacancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do during 2029 if thinking AI arrived in 2028?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If no place opened by 2029, I'd keep operating and volunteer for a supervised diagnostics shift. I would apply for a posted technician vacancy rather than assume the course will create one.

say: I expect thinking AI to plan shifts by **2028**, with loader robots around 2031.
I want operators to have paid training and a **transfer path**.
think: My lead planning tasks could go quickly, while physical work gets a **three-year window**.
I know AI experience cannot stop a robot from taking the **loader job**.
do: Ask mine management for the **transfer list** now.
Take a paid diagnostics course in 2029 if it leads to an **open role**.
feel: I feel **anxious** about fast change, but not trapped by it.
S2.quote: I cannot learn my way out of a robot taking the loader job.
fieldNote: Kira distinguishes her comfort with AI from the later **robot exposure** of her core work.
Outside household **income** gives her some room to seek a transfer.
She will not spend savings without a paid course tied to a **vacancy**.

steps.text: Ask the mine and worker representatives for transfer openings
Take the paid diagnostics course if a vacancy is linked
Keep operating while the course or post is confirmed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew five years is enough time to test a new path before AGI arrives in 2031. Loader robots follow around 2034, so we should know which mine roles are expected to remain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can learn the control and diagnostics tools quickly, but physical jobs remain my main pay. Inspection may help for a while, yet robots could eventually do those checks too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the mine's equipment-diagnostics course and ask to shadow the reliability team. In 2032, I would apply for a posted maintenance role if it includes hands-on fault work, while keeping my loader shifts until an offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel concerned, not defeated. Five years lets me build skills, though I will check whether the next mine has the same needs before moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which skill would you want to carry to another mine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the diagnostics skills and equipment logs with me to another mine. I would ask whether their technicians still inspect faults in person instead of assuming a certificate will transfer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do during 2032, the first year after AGI arrived?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2032, I would ask the reliability lead what work has been automated and apply only for tasks the team still needs a person to perform. I would stay on the loader roster until the new role was confirmed.

say: I think five years is enough time to test a path before **2031**.
I want to map which mine roles remain before robots arrive around **2034**.
think: I can learn diagnostics quickly, but physical jobs remain my main **pay**.
I know inspection might help temporarily; robots could take those **checks** later.
do: Take the mine equipment **diagnostics course** and shadow reliability staff.
Apply in 2032 for a posted maintenance role with hands-on **fault work**.
feel: I feel **concerned**, but five years gives me room to build skills.
S3.quote: Inspection may help for a while, yet robots could eventually do those checks too.
fieldNote: She makes training conditional on **hands-on fault work** remaining.
Kira recognizes inspection as exposed to later **robot progress**.
Nearby mines offer options, but she would verify whether her skills **transfer**.

steps.text: Apply for a maintenance role with human fault work
Keep loader shifts until the new role is confirmed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade lets us prepare if the mine is honest about staffing. AGI comes in 2036, then loader robots around 2039, so the equipment work has longer but not endless runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 53 and 56 at those dates, and I expect to still need wages. I can move toward reliability work, but I would keep checking whether robots are taking those tasks too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the diagnostics course while staying on the loader roster and save a set amount from each overtime payment. In 2037, I would apply for a reliability post only if its duties still need a person on site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The extra years make me feel more in control. They do not make me certain about a job after 2039, so I'd want the mine to update workers each year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your children to learn before 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2037, the children will be young adults, and Karim and I would help them compare training with employers beyond mining. I would not tell them to choose the mine just because I know it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do during 2037, the first year after AGI arrived?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the reliability manager which tasks remain human-led and check openings at the other nearby mines. If I had to move, I would compare a signed job offer with the children's plans and mortgage first.

say: I see a decade to prepare if the mine is honest about **staffing**.
I know loader work has a longer runway, but it is not **endless**.
think: At 53 and 56, I will still need **wages**.
I expect reliability work may also change as robots take more **tasks**.
do: Finish the diagnostics course while keeping the **loader roster**.
Save overtime and apply in 2037 for a reliability post with human **duties**.
feel: The extra time gives me **control**, but not certainty about work after 2039.
S4.quote: The extra years make me feel more in control.
fieldNote: She expects to keep earning and learns toward **reliability work**.
Kira will check each year whether robots are also taking **inspection tasks**.
She expects her children to be young adults by **2037** and supports wider options.

steps.text: Complete the diagnostics course while operating the loader
Save a fixed amount from each overtime payment
Apply for a reliability post with human duties in 2037
Help the children compare training beyond mining

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year picture worries me because the planning work changes before there is much time to prepare for robots. A paid course, a clear transfer list and a say in how the mine changes targets would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I would want managers to tell crews which jobs are changing and when, and let us test tools before they become mandatory. I can learn new systems, but safe work still needs a person to check the machine.

headlineQuote: I can learn new systems, but safe work still needs a person to check the machine.
portrait: Kira is a 43-year-old senior mine operator with a **technical diploma**.
She uses AI daily and is quick to test **new tools** at work.
Her partner works outside mining; they have two children, a mortgage and **moderate savings**.
She pursues diagnostics and reliability work while questioning how long **robots** leave those tasks to people.
biggestWorry: The **two-year AGI** picture worries her because shift planning could change before a family can prepare for robots.
whatWouldHelp: Paid **courses**, a clear transfer list and worker input on targets would help Kira plan.
